SERVICE.finding: Stated on the packet's own face. The SCA-C906 certificate of service page names all five statutory recipients by office — the Superintendent of the State Police, the County Prosecuting Attorney's Office, the Chief of Police or other executive head of the municipal police department where the offence occurred, the chief law-enforcement officer of any other agency that participated in the arrest, and the superintendent or warden of any institution of confinement — with an address rule for each, and it names the methods: First Class Mail, Hand Delivery, Certified Mail – Return Receipt. The SCA-C900 instructions component adds the direction to make as many copies as are needed to serve all parties by the method indicated, and states the § 61-11-26(e) opposition window. The instructions correctly leave the certificate blank until service has happened.

SELF_HELP_STOP.finding: Met on the narrow reading. The instructions state which facts the platform will not supply — eleven named groups, opening "Do not file until every item below is completed on the operative SCA-C906 petition from your own records. Do not guess." — and which fields it will not sign: "The participant signature, signature date, verification/notary completion, and the entire certificate of service remain blank and protected." They also carry a substantive stop the source demands: do not complete or file SCA-C900's embedded outdated petition instead of SCA-C906. There is no not-legal-advice paragraph; the control plane carries the no-approval half — approval-request.json records status REQUESTED, generationAllowed false, runtimeSelectable false, independentVisualReviewRequired true, outputLegalApprovalRequired true, zero commercial routes opened.

FEE_AND_WAIVER.finding: The packet tells the participant that it does not state an amount that its own delivered pages print. participant-instructions.md carries, in bold: "The BCI certificate carries a separate fee, and this packet does not state an amount because BCI sets it per applicant." The canonical fixture this family ships prints "$65.00" three times on packet pages 17 and 18, on the BCI Application for Certificate of Eligibility the packet itself delivers. DET-FEE-AND-WAIVER-001 amendment A4 states the rule in one line: a packet may never tell a participant that it does not state something it does state. A SECOND and independent limb fails here, and it is the A1/A2/A3 one rather than A4's internal-consistency rule. The compiled Utah state profile (src/lib/rcap-engine/compiled/profiles/UT-utah.json, SHA-256 73dd7ea988d0673dca3b8bf657f2df090d062c0821f8c0662a57ccfac8e7660d) states: "eligible conviction, plea-in-abeyance, or special certificates may require an additional $65 per case; no certificate issuance fee is required for dismissals, acquittals, or declinations." This route is a dismissal without prejudice. Applying A3's per-fact, per-route test rather than reading the document as a whole: the exempting limb names "dismissals" without qualification, and the limb that does carry a charge names conviction, plea-in-abeyance and special certificates, none of which is this route. A dismissal without prejudice is a dismissal and is not a plea in abeyance, so the exemption reaches it. The repository therefore establishes that the certificate issuance fee for this route is nil, and A2 lists the compiled state profile for the family's jurisdiction as a held source in its own right. The packet nonetheless tells the participant that it cannot state the amount and sends them to ask BCI — which is precisely what A1 forbids where the record already answers. The residual ambiguity is stated rather than resolved: the profile's word is "dismissals", unqualified, and a lane wanting certainty should read the BCI FAQ the profile cites before publishing $0. onWhetherAnA4BreachIsMechanicallyDisting.questionAsked: Captain asked whether a detector can tell a legitimate refusal from a false denial, since R17's three repaired families state the $65.00 AND keep a refusal about the certificate amount, and a naive detector reads both shapes the same.
onWhetherAnA4BreachIsMechanicallyDisting.answer: Yes for A4, and the rule is cheap, local and needs no source hunt. It is NOT sufficient for the fee obligation as a whole, and the difference matters more than the answer.
onWhetherAnA4BreachIsMechanicallyDisting.theRuleForA4: A4 is a claim about the packet's own contents, so the check is closed over the packet. A refusal sentence carries a SUBJECT — the thing whose amount is not stated. A breach exists when the packet prints an amount FOR THAT SAME SUBJECT. So: extract the refusal's subject noun phrase; extract every amount in the delivered artifact together with the noun phrase the artifact's own line attaches it to; breach if and only if the two subjects are the same referent. Applied here it separates the two shapes exactly. The three subject families refuse for "the BCI certificate" while their pages print "$65.00" attached to "the application fee" — which looks like an escape until the packet's own prose is read: it never distinguishes the two, so a reader has one BCI amount in mind and finds a different one printed, and that is the defect. R17's repaired families refuse for "the certificates themselves" AFTER stating "the BCI application fee is $65.00" for the other subject and saying in terms that BCI charges two separate amounts. Same tokens, different referents, and the discriminator is whether the packet has itself drawn the distinction before relying on it.
onWhetherAnA4BreachIsMechanicallyDisting.theMechanicalTestThatActuallyWorks: The referent test above can be run without natural-language subject extraction, which is where a gate would otherwise get expensive and unreliable. Reduce it to: does the packet's participant-facing text state EVERY distinct amount that its own delivered pages print, or explicitly name and set aside each one it is not talking about? Both are string operations over two artifacts the family already ships. A packet that prints $65.00 and never writes "$65.00" in its instructions, while also denying that it states an amount, fails. A packet that prints $65.00, writes "$65.00" in its instructions, and then refuses a DIFFERENT amount it never prints, passes. That is a sound decision procedure for the A4 class specifically, and it produces no false positive on R17's three.
onWhetherAnA4BreachIsMechanicallyDisting.whereItIsNotSufficient: The rule is closed over the packet, so it can only see contradictions the packet contains. It cannot see a refusal that is internally consistent and still false because the REPOSITORY holds the answer — the A1/A2/A3 failure. Two of the three families scored above fail on exactly that second limb: the compiled Utah state profile establishes that no certificate issuance fee is required for dismissals and declinations, so their certificate refusal would survive the A4 test above and still be wrong.
